name: Pax Romana: Infrastructure and Travel

objectives.text: Identify pictures of the ways people traveled in Bible times, such as walking on stone roads and sailing in boats
Retell how Paul traveled by road and by ship to tell people in many places about Jesus
Describe what a Roman road looked like and explain why the Romans built such strong, straight roads
Explain in your own words that Pax Romana means Roman Peace, a long period when Rome kept order across many lands beginning in the time of Caesar Augustus
Explain how roads, sea routes, and peace across the empire helped early missionaries carry the gospel from city to city
Compare travel in the first century with travel today in speed, cost, comfort, and danger
Trace Paul's first missionary journey on a map, naming the cities he visited and whether he traveled by land or sea
Describe how Rome's control of the Mediterranean, including the clearing of pirates and the grain ships from Alexandria, shaped sea travel in Paul's day
Explain how Roman administration, such as the census, required people to travel, using the journey of Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem
Analyze how major Roman roads such as the Via Egnatia and the Via Appia connected the cities named in Acts
Explain how the shared Koine Greek language allowed travelers and missionaries to communicate across the eastern empire
Interpret the phrase fullness of time in its context in Galatians and explain why many interpreters connect it to the conditions of the Roman world
Explain the role of Roman colonies like Philippi as settlements of Roman citizens along major roads and how Luke describes the city
Describe how Jewish communities and synagogues in cities along trade routes served as starting points for Paul's preaching
Construct a map of Paul's journeys showing the roads and sea routes he likely used, citing the passages in Acts that support each route
Analyze how Roman travel networks made it possible for letters and messengers to link scattered churches
Evaluate the cost and danger of first-century travel despite the Roman peace, using Paul's own account of his hardships
Explain the Reformed doctrine that God governs history through ordinary means and apply it to the conditions surrounding Christ's coming and the spread of the gospel
Evaluate historical arguments that credit the early church's growth to Roman conditions, distinguishing secondary causes from God's providence as the Reformed tradition confesses it
Synthesize the roads, sea routes, common language, colonies, and peace of the Roman world into a written argument about how they shaped the early church's mission

changes: Kept and reworded real competencies (Roman roads, Paul's travel, Pax Romana, roads and gospel spread, then and now comparison, road network, fullness of time, Koine, Philippi, journey map, cost and danger, providence, synthesis). Dropped filler (naming a boat, observing safety). Reframed the piracy item as a description of Roman sea control. Replaced 'defend providential timing' with explaining and evaluating the Reformed doctrine of providence through secondary causes. Added the census journey, a first journey map task, diaspora synagogues on trade routes, and letters carried along Roman networks. Anchored objectives to specific verses in Acts, Luke, Galatians, 2 Corinthians and the Epistles, and to WCF 5.1-5.3 and Heidelberg Q27 where they state providence.
